parsed_answer.content: When dealing with full-text search and inverted index architectures (such as Elasticsearch or Apache Lucene), three foundational concepts govern how raw string data is ingested, structured, and queried: Mappings, Analyzers, and Tokenizers. Mappings act as the schema definition for documents, dictating how fields are typed, indexed, and stored in the underlying index structure. Analyzers are complete text-processing pipelines composed of zero or more character filters, exactly one tokenizer, and zero or more token filters. They dictate how text is transformed during both ingestion (indexing) and search phases. At the core of every analyzer sits the Tokenizer, the specific engine responsible for breaking a raw text stream down into discrete token units, such as individual words, by chopping the stream up based on whitespace, punctuation, or custom regular expressions.

items: Mappings dictate whether a string field is treated as a 'text' field (subject to full-text analysis and inverted index creation) or a 'keyword' field (exact-match, unanalyzed doc-values storage).
Tokenizers consume a character stream, emit a stream of token objects with positional increments and offset metadata, and can never be chained or multiplied within a single analyzer configuration.

Custom analyzers allow engineers to combine character filters (like HTML stripters), specific tokenizers (like standard or edge_ngram), and token filters (like lowercase, stemmers, or synonyms) to match domain-specific search requirements.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap in full-text search systems is asymmetric analysis: configuring an analyzer for the indexing phase that differs from the query phase analyzer. If you stem words or strip punctuation during indexing using an aggressive tokenizer/filter combination but fail to apply the identical transformation chain to the search query text, users will experience zero-hit search anomalies.
